words: Yeah, I think we do.

words: That's a real advantage, yeah.

words: You mean like...

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: And so he'll have some choices.

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: Right. I hope he has, you know, a few ideas on life and stuff. I'm sure he will. I'm sure by then he'll have a lot of ideas we didn't even dream of. Probably lots of occupations will be opened up that we didn't know about, but now, you know.

words: How do you see... Do you see the role of children as having changed from the time you were growing up to what... Of course, you haven't had a child very long, and Eric isn't much into his role yet. Do you see any differences in that respect?

words: The only thing...I don't know if this is how it was when I was little or nothing, but the only thing I noticed is a few of my girlfriends that have babies, you know, they're all constantly comparing. I don't want to compare him with anybody or anything.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So they're kind of pushing their...

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: Right. Grow up, grow up, grow up, you know. I want Eric to stay with me.

words: Do you think it has anything to do with their sense of being a better achievement, being a better mother because their children are potty trained faster than yours?

words: I think so. I talked to my doctor about potty trained talking, you know, and walking and stuff like that. He just says when Eric is ready, he'll let you know. speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you think these other mothers have maybe put some stress on their child?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: I think so. Now, you know, maybe I'm sitting in judgment or something, but I just hope I don't compare him.

words: He's just bragging to me, you know. Yeah. But the doctor seems to have a sense of this, too. Right. So he's encouraging you just to let Eric go at his own pace. Right. Mm-hmm. words: But he's got this new job now, so he works longer hours and stuff. So we don't, during the week, we just kind of stay home, and he goes bitter and stuff. words: That's another advantage to being in the outfield, that you're closer to where you can do that.

words: He loves to do that stuff so much. We do that. That's mostly what we do. Because if you want to go to the shower, sometimes you try to clean the moss off.

words: It gets red. Yeah, you wonder if it's worth all that trip.

words: Like money and tire gas.

words: It does take a lot of money, too.

words: Gas and your meals and the show. Mm-hmm. We go once in a while, but not very often.

words: You have to be pretty sure the show is good enough for that, don't you?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: Right, right.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Mm-hmm. Is it you— Did your family do things together as you were growing up more, or do you anticipate that you and Eric and his father will do— will there be a change there?

words: I had the kids most of the time, so they went off for their recreation.

words: Some people just think, you know, I think I'd like the three of us to do stuff together. Mm-hmm. So we'd be there all the time. Did you feel left out? Well, really they were probably gone, you know, a few hours downtown or something, you know, but I don't know. I don't think I felt left out as much as I wanted to go, you know, see what they were doing and stuff, maybe. But I wanted to take Eric with us because what we do, he might as well go, you know, and there's no reason to leave him home. Mm-hmm. speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Did he? He played pool? Mm-hmm. He participated?

words: He liked that real well. Did you? I did. He did too. I did the first few weekends, and then I didn't because it was just mainly guys. It wasn't as much fun as it would have been with a bunch of girls, you know. Uh-huh.

words: Do you enjoy things with other girls now? Uh-huh. You get together, like your birthday clubs and that kind of thing. Mm-hmm. And you just get together socially, I suppose, with others.

words: Right, yeah.

words: It would be kind of damaging to him to have a woman supporting him. Would that be there, too?

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: For sure. Uh-huh. Do you ever hear your mother talk about the war years, the depression, your grandmother talk about the depression years?

words: My mom doesn't like us to ever buy anything on credit because they went through it, I think.

words: I don't believe it. The credits I don't believe is this here third party, which is finance. Where if I go buy a stove from Sears and Roebuck, I don't like for them to put on another finance. Okay, we got the TV. They took our older man for $25, which should have been at least $100, but they only gave us $25, which couldn't help. Come to find out when we had to get it, it was over $300 or more because it went through, oh, I always forget that. Avco? No, the other one. Inofficial? No, they have it all over. I think it kind of went out of commission anyway. And I don't believe, when I was, the first year we were married, John was for everything. We have to have money for this. I said, why? Because we can't pay cash flow, so we'll borrow the money. And I said, where are you going to borrow from? The finance company. Isn't that funny? I can't think of the other finance companies. So I'd write this whole thing, get money, maybe $100. Well, it would take $150 to pay it back. So I got, I said, if we ever get out of debt, I'll never, ever, ever want to go eating with a third party. I just don't like it. You pay $150 for something, you have to pay maybe $250. Well, it's not doing you any good. It's just doing them good. Isn't that crazy? I cannot think of that.

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: We just went and bought a TV and a bed. We've been wanting a new bed. Our bed was 15 years old, and it had it. Just the price brings it.

words: I like to see people, I love Norma June's beautiful furniture. But we can't afford it until we can afford it, like we just have to get along with the old stuff we got. You know? But this year, from buying this secondhand, this has been old, maybe four or five years ago. But when you buy, find out one thing. If you buy a secondhand thing, you're buying somebody else's troubles. There was a reason why they got rid of it. You bet. You bet. That's another thing that's...

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: Steve really hates to buy a charge or any of that. He always wants to save up the money. That's getting pretty tough to do, though, nowadays, to save up that money and live at the same time for something. And they know it, too. They got you over a barrel. If you want it bad enough, they'll give it to you one way or the other.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you feel as though you still remember some things from the Depression. Oh, you bet I do. One thing for sure I can remember at Depression time. We had a washing machine, which I needed desperately. I was pregnant with Norma, our middle girl. The other girl was lit real little. And I only had $8 to pay on it. One dollar was as much now as $100 today. Do you know I couldn't scrape enough to get $5 to pay on my washing machine? I asked several people in town. No, they wouldn't give it to you. He made $36 a month. And sometimes you didn't get that. Or I don't know what happened, but I think they just... We just waited and told them that we'd pay it next month, next month, until we finally put $2, $3 on it. And I didn't lose my washing machine. But that's the kind of instant that we were in, you know, at Depression time. And at that time you couldn't get... for everything, to get even a piece of bread and stuff on the table for your children. Really, we only had the one child. Norma, she was born then. And I can remember when she was born. We lived in a little shack. We paid, I think we paid $13 a month, which was, at that time, was pretty hard. And there was a big forest fire out here. And she didn't sleep well, very good. And her dad had to go to work at 3 o'clock in the morning. And she was much fresher like most babies are. And I kept her in the back in the bedroom, and I knelt in the bedroom into the kitchen. And there were cinders on our porch. We went out there at one time, being goodbyed, there were cinders on the front porch. And they come to us and says, if you want to live, if this place, if this town burns up, you want to live, you go, we have to all get together and go up to the river and stay out to the riverbank because to save your life. Well, I had two babies. I just, it was really, and my husband had a frightened fire and stuff, and that was really bad at that time. And, well, and she was only about three months old, three weeks old, I think. And there's a lot of things I can remember. What did you do then? Well, it wasn't, we didn't get that bad. We just, they would go out 3 o'clock in the morning and see my son. He had to go to fight the fire. And, but they finally got it out. It seemed like they didn't have the facility to put out a fire like they do now out in the woods. You know, they drop stuff down and it kind of smothers it. At that time, they didn't have all that stuff. There was an in-power. Well, that's kind of some of the stuff I do remember. I like, I can remember when we first came to Elk River, too. A lot of the stuff that goes on before we ever got to Elk River as far as that's concerned. Well, let's finish up the song before she has to leave for the baby, and then we'll get to your story. words: Right, to do. You have to be able to think of stuff. Like a lot of us, we play cards all the time.

words: Do you and your husband make decisions together? Is there an area that he makes decisions about, or how do you handle things like that?

words: I think we do make decisions together. We talk it over a lot before we ever make major decisions anyway. Like as far as his job goes, he does that pretty much on his own. He knows what makes him happy and sad.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: How about the spending of the money and everything? Do you both do that?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: I keep books. I take a deal from him. We talk it over a bit. I do most of it. Like if we have $20 and I can decide where it goes, I make the decision and he doesn't have to.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: He trusts you then, in your judgment. Is there anything that he decides and you wish you had more influence with him on some things or do you just speak up when you...

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: I just tell him.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So that's just what you would... No.

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: He doesn't... We can walk through his bars of decision as we take. He doesn't ever just go out and do, you know, buy anything without me with him.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Who decided that you were going to live here in Mount Priebus? Was it his job or...

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: It was his job. I think we would... If he didn't have a job here, I mean, he could have found one in Pollack. I think he might have lived there the longest. I could have worked a little bit longer, but I don't know. I think it was probably his job. He's worked on the fire patrol at the time and then he got on year-round as a foreman. So we came here. We found a house here before we got married. So... Which means... We both liked it here, you know. That wasn't the only reason we stayed here.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: What differences do you see between yourself and the girls who didn't go away to school?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: There's narrow-minded... I'll say that over and over. I've had a lot of things. Narrow-minded and not, you know... I mean, I don't know everything, you know. I didn't live in San Francisco long enough to really know a lot about it. Like, they talk about the city. They don't know, really, what it's like. That's in five days, something. And they don't know what it's like to go on to school. They don't know how hard it is to have to cram a year's work into four months, four hours a day, you know. Just stay away from home all that time. That's the main thing I get disgusted at is because they think they know it all. They don't. About going away and city life.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do they see it as something desirable?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: They see it as a big bunch of fun and glamour and going away to the river and stuff.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you experienced it. It was not just that glamorous.

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: And I hate to say, you know, like, open your eyes, it isn't all that great. I don't want to discourage them, but still, they should know what...

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Are they saying they'd like to go live in the city? They'd like to get out of Elk River?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: Yes, a lot of them say, oh, I don't know why anybody wants to stay in Elk River, but yet they stay.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Do they not see a way to get away with them?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: No person's job is here.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So they feel kind of like they're in prison.

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: But personally, I think if... Like, if Steve and I decided we wanted to get away, I think one of us could find a good enough job to get us out of here if we wanted to. That's it. Just sitting on it.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: Well, that takes care of most of the questions I had to ask you. Would you like to add anything else? How do you feel about... Have you ever any time wished you were not a girl?

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: No, I like being a girl. I like it. I'd rather be treated like I'm treated now rather than, you know... I can do good things in a woman's world, but, you know, I don't want to change too much. I like being the housewife, cooking the meals and cleaning the house, taking care of Eric. I think I'd miss a lot of times at work when Eric was little. I'd kind of go back to work because, like, I have both my kids and they're in school, and they won't need me so much, you know. And I like being like I am.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: So you're pretty well pleased with what... Yeah. With your situation now. Yeah. Anything else you'd like to add about Elk River or...

speaker: Sonja Christine Clyne
words: I can't think of anything. If I think I could say it, I can't think of it now.

speaker: Isabel Miller
words: You can't think of anything right now. I think we've covered quite a bit. A lot, yeah. Yeah. Okay, we'll... I just couldn't make a living here, so...
